questions.explain: Orchestration answers what needs to run, in what order, and under what conditions — a single cron job running a backup at 2 AM is scheduling, not orchestration. Orchestration begins when tasks have dependencies between them.
options: Managing conditional, multi-step workflows with dependencies between tasks — what runs, in what order, under what conditions
Running a single cron job that executes a backup script at 2 AM
Scheduling every maintenance job with the native scheduler and no logging
Executing all tasks simultaneously to finish maintenance windows faster
questions.q: How does the chapter distinguish orchestration from mere scheduling?

questions.explain: The chapter's job-history query decodes msdb run_status: 0 = Failed, 1 = Succeeded, 2 = Retry, 3 = Cancelled, 4 = In Progress — history stored in sysjobs, sysjobsteps, and sysjobhistory in msdb.
options: The job is scheduled but has never executed
The job succeeded with warnings
The job step was retried
The job was cancelled by the operator
questions.q: In msdb's sysjobhistory, what does run_status = 2 mean?

questions.explain: The chapter's maintenance-pipeline query classifies indexes with avg_fragmentation_in_percent >= 30 as REBUILD, >= 10 as REORGANIZE, else SKIP (with page_count > 1000), then fans out rebuild/reorganize tasks per index.
options: REBUILD for any fragmentation above 5%, regardless of page count
REORGANIZE only; REBUILD is never recommended in an automated pipeline
SKIP for everything above 30% because rebuilds are too risky
REBUILD at 30% or more, REORGANIZE at 10% or more (for indexes over 1000 pages)
questions.q: What fragmentation thresholds does the chapter's index-maintenance pipeline use for REBUILD vs REORGANIZE?

questions.explain: Flyway and Liquibase express migrations as versioned, ordered scripts with checksums that prevent modification after application, tracking which migrations were applied per environment; the orchestration layer runs the migration tool at the right deployment point with pre-checks and post-validation.
options: Storing migration scripts in a shared folder that DBAs run by hand on deployment night
Versioned, ordered scripts with per-migration checksums, applied by the orchestration layer with pre-migration checks and post-validation
Embedding ALTER TABLE statements directly in application code with no tracking
Applying migrations with sp_cdc_change_job so the distribution database validates them
questions.q: How should schema migrations be incorporated into deployment pipelines, per the chapter?

questions.explain: An index rebuild failing on a conflicting lock should retry with exponential backoff (e.g., 5, 15, 45 minutes). Flat retry intervals cause thundering-herd problems when multiple parallel tasks fail simultaneously and all retry at the same moment.
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop until the lock is released
Retry with exponential backoff (e.g., 5, 15, 45 minutes) to avoid thundering-herd retries
Skip the failed rebuild permanently and log it as a warning
Abort the entire pipeline, because a failed rebuild can never be retried safely
questions.q: An orchestrated index rebuild fails because a long-running transaction holds a conflicting lock. What retry strategy does the chapter recommend?
